subject: OpenAI shelves its IPO as AI bosses urge a slowdown
bodyMarkdown:
Three men who run rival AI labs spent the weekend agreeing with each other, and by Sunday night it had moved money. US stock futures were lower before dawn this morning, and the most anticipated share sale in tech just slipped to next year.

## What Amodei actually asked for

CNBC reported on Saturday that Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published an essay saying "we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," and that building too fast is reckless. His plan has three steps. First, let outside evaluators inside the company with employee-level access so they can check safety practices and report incidents, which Anthropic says it has already committed to on its own. Second, get labs in democratic countries to agree on shared safety standards. Third, extend that coordination to authoritarian governments. Sam Altman posted on X that independent evaluators with employee-like access is "a great idea, and we will do the same." Elon Musk backed the essay too. CNBC reported on Sunday that Amodei calls China the toughest dilemma in the whole plan, which sounds right to me, because step one is checkable and steps two and three are wishes.

## The IPO calendar moved first

Altman told Fortune in an interview published Saturday that going public now would come at "an ill-advised moment," and OpenAI confirmed it will not list this year, CNBC reported. That is a fast reversal. A month ago OpenAI finance chief Sarah Friar told staff the company would be public by 2027 or sooner. Anthropic is walking the other way. CNBC reported on Monday that it has picked the Nasdaq, plans to start marketing its offering in mid-October at the earliest, and wants to list in the days before the November midterm elections, with investors pushing for a valuation near $2 trillion against the $965 billion it was worth earlier this year. The Globe and Mail reported that the number rests on Anthropic projecting roughly $190 billion to $200 billion of revenue in 2028.

## How the market read it

**Stock futures**, the contracts traders use to bet on where an index will open, fell overnight. CNBC had S&P 500 futures down 0.6% and Nasdaq 100 futures down 1.44% at 3:06 a.m. Eastern, with Dow futures off about 50 points. Japan's Nikkei 225 closed down 0.81% and South Korea's Kospi dropped 3.26%. Oil is part of that, since Saudi Arabia shut a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi attacks disrupted another shipping lane, and dearer crude squeezes expensive tech shares through rates. Still, a decline concentrated in the Nasdaq while the Dow barely moves looks to me like the AI story rather than the oil one. Washington is not slowing down. Speaking in Ireland, President Trump said "we're leading China in AI ... and, frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

## The takeaway

The promise I would hold these companies to is the evaluator one, so watch the next few weeks for real names and access terms instead of posts on X. Anthropic's prospectus should land around mid-October, and its risk factors will tell you how seriously its lawyers take a self-imposed slowdown that costs revenue. The Fed decides on Wednesday, and Yahoo Finance reported this month that futures traders put the odds of a quarter point increase near 56%, which will do more to your account this week than any essay. If you bought the AI trade through a Nasdaq-heavy ETF, today is a good morning to ask whether you could sit through a 20% drawdown in it, because the people building the technology just told you they are less sure than they were a month ago.
